articles.title: NHS asks Rochdale families to help get patients home safely from hospital this winter
articles.excerpt: Families and friends are being asked to be ready to collect loved ones, prepare their homes and speak to ward teams early as North West NHS services work to get patients home sooner.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale families are being asked to help relatives leave hospital safely this winter as North West NHS services work to get patients home sooner.

NHS England says hospitals and community services across the region are working to make sure patients can leave hospital as soon as they are well enough. Families and friends can help by being ready to collect their loved ones when the time comes.

Returning to familiar surroundings with the right support in place can help people recover, regain their independence and get back to their usual routines. Staying in hospital longer than needed can increase the risk of infection and loss of strength and mobility.

Dr Michael Gregory, Regional Medical Director for NHS England in the North West, said: “For patients, going home is about getting back to the people and everyday life they know. This is something that can make a real difference to recovery. Families and friends can help make a difference by helping their loved ones take that next step.

“If you are worried about how someone will manage, please speak to the ward team early. We want to understand those concerns and what help you can offer, so we can plan together for a safe return home.”

Ward teams will work with patients and, where appropriate, their family, friends or unpaid carers to plan a safe discharge. They will discuss what support may be available and how to access it, and will aim for discharge earlier in the day where possible.

Before leaving, patients and those supporting them should understand the discharge plan, including any medicines, follow-up appointments and who to contact with concerns.

NHS England suggests families and friends check the expected discharge date and time with the ward team, and help arrange transport where possible.

Relatives can bring suitable clothes and shoes for the journey home, and check with the ward that medicines are ready and that their loved one understands how to take them.

At home, families can help by putting the heating on, making sure food and other essentials are available, and clearing walkways of clutter and trip hazards.

They should also make sure the patient knows who to contact if they need help.

Across the North West, specialist wards and services providing hospital-level care at home are helping patients leave hospital sooner. They include the Oasis Unit at Rochdale Infirmary, a specialist dementia ward featured in the same NHS England campaign.

Anyone who needs urgent medical help after returning home and is unsure where to turn can contact NHS 111 by phone or at 111.nhs.uk. For a life-threatening emergency, call 999.

Source: NHS England North West press office, press release issued on 24 November 2026.

What it means for Rochdale families

  • Families can check the expected discharge date and time with the ward team, and help arrange transport where possible.
  • Relatives can check with the ward that medicines are ready and that their loved one understands how to take them.
  • Anyone who needs urgent medical help after returning home and is unsure where to turn can contact NHS 111 by phone or at 111.nhs.uk.

articles.title: Rochdale Infirmary dementia care scheme cuts hospital stays by up to eight days
articles.excerpt: Specialist dementia wards including Rochdale Infirmary’s Oasis Unit are helping patients return home sooner, with average stays reduced by up to eight days.
articles.content_html:
A specialist dementia care model used at Rochdale Infirmary is helping patients return home sooner, with average hospital stays across the programme reduced by up to eight days, NHS England says.

The Oasis Unit at Rochdale Infirmary is one of three Northern Care Alliance services highlighted in a winter discharge campaign. Similar specialist dementia wards operate at Fairfield General Hospital in Bury and Salford Royal.

Patients living with dementia can remain on the same ward throughout their hospital stay, reducing moves that can be unsettling and allowing staff to provide care in a familiar environment. Activities are tailored to individual needs as part of the approach.

Northern Care Alliance information describes the Oasis Unit as a 10-bed medical ward for patients who have an acute medical condition and are also living with dementia. The unit includes colour-coordinated rooms and shared spaces designed to help with orientation and recovery.

NHS England said teams begin speaking with relatives early in a patient's stay and work with Age UK to arrange support for a safe return home. Across the specialist ward programme, the average length of stay has fallen by up to eight days.

Dr Michael Gregory, NHS England's Regional Medical Director for the North West, said: “Families and friends can help make a difference by helping their loved ones take that next step.”

The NHS is asking relatives and carers to discuss practical arrangements with hospital teams before a patient is ready to leave. This can include transport, suitable clothing, food at home and help with follow-up appointments or medicines.

For Rochdale families, early discharge planning can reduce delays once a patient is medically ready to leave hospital and make the move home safer.

articles.title: Inquest opens into death of three-year-old Thiago Wall from Middleton
articles.excerpt: An inquest has opened into the death of Thiago William Wall, who died after choking at Cosy Toes nursery in Middleton.
articles.content_html:
An inquest has opened into the death of Thiago William Wall, a three-year-old boy from Middleton, who died after choking on food at Cosy Toes nursery on Mainway East.

Thiago was rushed to the Royal Manchester Children's Hospital on 2 November, shortly after celebrating his third birthday on 26 October.

During the inquest at Rochdale Coroner's Court, it was revealed that Thiago was found choking with a bowl of food at the nursery. Despite medical efforts, he died on 5 November after suffering a hypoxic brain injury, which was deemed unsurvivable following a CT scan.

Senior coroner Joanne Kearsley expressed condolences to Thiago's family during the brief hearing and recorded a provisional cause of death as choking. "I am sure everybody would wish to express our condolences to Thiago's family," Ms Kearsley said.

In the wake of this tragedy, Cosy Toes nursery has closed its doors. Representatives from the nursery described Thiago as a wonderful and beautiful child, highlighting the profound impact of his loss on the community.

articles.title: You may be able to claim for Turner Brothers asbestos
articles.excerpt: Former workers, their families and people who lived near the Spotland factory can still claim, and there are routes for people exposed elsewhere too.
articles.content_html:
People made ill by asbestos from the former Turner Brothers Asbestos factory in Spotland can still claim compensation, 25 years after the company collapsed.

Former workers can claim, and so can people who never worked there, such as relatives exposed to dust on work clothes and people who lived near the factory.

Claims linked to Turner Brothers are handled by the T&N UK Asbestos Trust, which holds a separate fund for Turner Brothers claims. Its website is tandnasbestos.org.uk.

The trust usually pays a set share of a claim's full value rather than the whole amount.

People exposed to asbestos at other workplaces may also be able to claim, even if their employer closed long ago. Mesothelioma, a cancer caused by asbestos, often takes 40 to 50 years to show symptoms.

An employer's insurer is usually responsible even when the firm no longer exists. The Employers' Liability Tracing Office, at elto.org.uk, helps people find a former employer's insurer, though it does not pay compensation itself.

People diagnosed with mesothelioma who cannot trace a liable employer or insurer may be able to claim from the government's Diffuse Mesothelioma Payment Scheme, which pays according to age.

A government lump sum under the Pneumoconiosis etc. (Workers' Compensation) Act 1979 covers certain dust-related diseases when damages cannot be won from an employer, often because it has stopped trading. The claim form helpline is 0800 279 2322.

A separate 2008 mesothelioma scheme covers people exposed through a relative's work clothes, and people who cannot say where they were exposed but were exposed only in the UK.

Since 31 October 2026, dependants claiming under either government scheme after a sufferer died without claiming receive the full amount the sufferer would have been paid.

For a 60-year-old claimant under the 2008 scheme, that raises a dependant's payment from £24,526 to £56,656, according to the government. The change applies to new claims only.

Asbestos products were made at the Spodden Valley site from 1879 until 1998, and it was once the world's largest asbestos textile factory. Turner & Newall went into administration in 2001.

The site's owner, Spodden Park Ltd, began investigation works this month to map where asbestos is buried, ahead of a clean-up and redevelopment.

Compensation claims generally have to begin within three years of diagnosis, or within three years of a death. Some government payments must be claimed within 12 months.

The Greater Manchester Asbestos Victims Support Group, a registered charity, gives free advice on benefits and compensation to people with any asbestos-related disease, and runs support groups for patients and bereaved families.

The group can be contacted on 0161 258 0166, Monday to Friday from 9.30am to 4pm, or at info@gmavsg.org. Specialist asbestos solicitors can advise which routes apply, and many work on a no win, no fee basis.

Sources: T&N Asbestos Trustee Company, GOV.UK, Employers' Liability Tracing Office, Greater Manchester Asbestos Victims Support Group. Photograph: Rochdale Daily.

articles.title: Over 1,000 referred to GPs after free health checks in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: A community health initiative in Rochdale has revealed that half of participants were unaware they needed medical attention, with 1,000 undiagnosed conditions identified.
articles.content_html:
A community initiative offering free health checks across Rochdale, Heywood, and Middleton has identified 1,000 undiagnosed health conditions among participants. Launched on 31 October 2025, the programme has conducted 2,000 health checks, revealing that 50% of those tested were unaware they needed medical attention.

The Community Health Checks programme, commissioned by Rochdale Council and delivered by the Living Well Rochdale Cardiovascular Disease team, aims to improve access to essential health screenings.

Checks are conducted at various locations, including community venues, GP practices, workplaces, and local stores, making it easier for residents to receive health assessments.

Each health check includes blood pressure monitoring, height and weight measurements, and a finger-prick test for blood sugar and cholesterol levels. Participants also receive their Body Mass Index and an assessment to estimate their risk of developing cardiovascular disease over the next decade.

The initiative is designed to help identify potential health concerns early, preventing them from developing into more serious conditions. The Living Well Rochdale CVD team continues to engage with the community to promote health awareness and encourage residents to take advantage of these free services.

articles.title: Man rescued from house fire on Abbott Street in Castleton taken to hospital
articles.excerpt: A man was rescued from a first-floor bedroom during a house fire on Abbott Street in Castleton and taken to Royal Oldham Hospital.
articles.content_html:
A man was rescued from a house fire on Abbott Street in Castleton on Saturday afternoon and taken to Royal Oldham Hospital, fire crews have confirmed.

The blaze broke out at about 3pm on Saturday 21 November at the back of the first floor of a semi-detached house.

Firefighters wearing breathing apparatus went inside and rescued the man from a rear bedroom, a spokesperson for Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service said.

Three fire engines attended along with paramedics and police. The man was handed over to the care of paramedics, and crews worked with North West Ambulance Service and Greater Manchester Police to make the area safe.

A GMFRS spokesperson said: "He was then taken to Royal Oldham Hospital." Crews were in attendance for around two hours and 15 minutes.

Video posted on social media showed fire engines and an ambulance parked on the street on Saturday evening, with part of the pavement taped off.

Greater Manchester Police said it was aware of the incident but that the fire was not believed to be suspicious at this stage.

Rochdale Daily has asked Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service for comment on the cause of the fire.

articles.title: Life Without Limits gym relocates to new premises in Littleborough
articles.excerpt: Life Without Limits fitness centre has received planning permission to move to a larger facility on Stockton Street, allowing for expansion and new services.
articles.content_html:
Life Without Limits fitness centre has been granted permission to relocate to a new site at 3a and 3b Stockton Street, Littleborough, as it continues to expand its services.

The gym, which currently operates from Unit 12a on the Paragon Industrial Estate, will move to a larger facility that will allow it to consolidate and expand its offerings, including group exercise, personal training, physiotherapy, and wellbeing services.

Joshua Smith, the applicant, noted in the planning documents that the business has grown significantly since its establishment and currently employs around 12 staff members. The new premises could potentially double the workforce as the business develops further.

This relocation is part of a broader trend of growth for the independent gym, which aims to better serve the community's fitness needs and enhance its service offerings.

articles.title: Rochdale teenagers born in 2009 or later will never be legally sold tobacco from 1 January
articles.excerpt: The generational smoking ban starts on 1 January 2027, making it an offence to sell tobacco to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009.
articles.content_html:
Young people in Rochdale borough born on or after 1 January 2009 will never be legally sold tobacco once the generational smoking ban takes effect on 1 January 2027.

The Department of Health and Social Care began a countdown to the change on Monday 16 November, with a campaign run jointly with the NHS.

From 1 January 2027 it becomes an offence to sell tobacco, herbal smoking products or cigarette papers to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009, under the Tobacco and Vapes Act 2026.

The cut-off does not move. In practice, the legal age for buying tobacco rises by one year every year, so the first group affected, who turn 18 during 2027, will never be able to buy it.

Anyone born before 1 January 2009 can still be sold tobacco as now.

The department described the law as "a once-in-a-generation opportunity to protect future generations from tobacco addiction".

When the bill became law in April, Health Secretary Wes Streeting said: "This legislation marks a turning point for the nation's health."

Shops selling tobacco will have to check whether customers were born on or after 1 January 2009.

They must also display a new notice stating: "It is illegal to sell tobacco products to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009."

The Act received Royal Assent on 29 April 2026. It also bans advertising and sponsorship of vapes and nicotine products, and gives ministers powers to restrict packaging and displays that appeal to children.

A retail licensing scheme and stronger action against illicit tobacco and vapes are also part of the law, according to the government.

Smoking causes about 80,000 deaths a year in the UK and is the leading preventable cause of death, the government says. There are an estimated 5.3 million smokers in the UK.

Rochdale has a higher smoking rate than England as a whole. Rochdale Borough Council's needs assessment puts it at 15.3 per cent of adults in 2021, against 12.7 per cent nationally.

A YouGov survey in August 2024 found 61 per cent of UK adults supported the ban for those born on or after 1 January 2009, with 27 per cent against.

The ban comes into force on Friday 1 January 2027.

Source: Department of Health and Social Care Facebook post, 16 November 2026; GOV.UK; Tobacco and Vapes Act 2026; Rochdale Borough Council Joint Strategic Needs Assessment. Photograph: UK Government / NHS.

What changes in Rochdale

  • From 1 January 2027 it becomes an offence to sell tobacco, herbal smoking products or cigarette papers to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009.
  • Anyone born before 1 January 2009 can still be sold tobacco as now.
  • Shops selling tobacco will have to check whether customers were born on or after 1 January 2009.

articles.title: Laced vapes: what is in them, how they reach children, and how to report sellers
articles.excerpt: Vapes sold to children as cannabis oil are being found to contain spice, a far stronger synthetic drug that has put young people in hospital. Here is what is known and how to report sellers in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
Vapes sold to children as cannabis oil are being found to contain spice, a synthetic drug far stronger than the cannabis it imitates, and young people across England have ended up in hospital after using them.

The vapes are usually advertised as “THC” liquid, the active ingredient in cannabis. Dealers swap in spice without telling buyers because it is cheaper, and its strength is unpredictable.

Research by Professor Chris Pudney, of the University of Bath, found in 2025 that as many as one in four vapes confiscated in schools contained spice.

He has identified a network of about 10,000 social media accounts linked to selling it, with “THC vape liquid” advertised for as little as £2. A genuine THC vape typically costs £60 to £80.

In June, ITV News reported the case of a boy who began using what he thought was a THC vape at 12. After about two months of daily use he collapsed, suffered a collapsed lung and spent two weeks in an induced coma.

In Hull, two 13-year-old girls were taken to hospital in April after being handed a vape at a park. Tests found spice and MDMA, according to their mother.

Most of the selling happens on social media, including Snapchat, TikTok and Instagram. Professor Pudney described it as overt drug dealing, with the platforms used as shop windows.

TikTok and Snapchat both say illegal vape sales are banned on their platforms and that they remove such content. Ofcom, which regulates the platforms under the Online Safety Act, says selling drugs to children is illegal and that it will act where platforms fall short.

In Rochdale borough, the council's trading standards team obtained closure orders against six shops in six months to December 2025 for illegal tobacco and vapes, including the Green Shop in Heywood, where illegal vapes were found in the shop and in a car linked to the business.

In June, Rochdale's neighbourhood police and trading standards carried out checks on shops in Milnrow and Littleborough for sales of vapes and alcohol to under-18s, and said the checks would continue regularly.

Parents are advised to warn children never to accept or share a vape from someone they do not know. If a child collapses, has a seizure or struggles to breathe after vaping, call 999.

Information about people selling drugs can be given to Greater Manchester Police on 101 or online at gmp.police.uk, or anonymously to Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

Sources: ITV News; University of Bath; Rochdale Borough Council; Greater Manchester Police. Photograph: Rochdale Daily library.

articles.title: Measles: the symptoms to look out for in your child, and when to get help
articles.excerpt: More than 1,000 measles cases have been confirmed in England this year, 111 of them in the North West. Here is how the illness starts and the warning signs that need urgent care.
articles.content_html:
Parents in Rochdale borough are being reminded what measles looks like, after 1,030 confirmed cases in England between 1 January and 12 October this year.

The North West accounted for 111 of those cases, about 11% of the national total, according to UK Health Security Agency figures.

Two measles-related deaths were confirmed in England earlier this year, both of them children, the agency said in June.

Measles usually starts like a cold, the NHS says. Early signs are a high temperature, a runny or blocked nose, sneezing, a cough, and red, sore, watery eyes.

A few days later, small white spots can appear inside the cheeks and on the back of the lips.

A rash follows a few days after the cold-like symptoms. It starts on the face and behind the ears before spreading over the body, and is usually not itchy.

On white skin the rash looks brown or red. On brown and black skin it can be harder to see.

People with measles are infectious from about four days before the rash appears until four days after it appears.

The NHS advises getting an urgent GP appointment or calling 111 if your child may have measles, has a high temperature that does not come down with paracetamol or ibuprofen, is struggling to breathe, or is feeding or weeing less than usual.

Parents should also seek urgent advice if a baby under one has been in contact with measles.

Ring the GP surgery before going in, so staff can arrange a phone appointment or see your child away from other patients.

Call 999 or go to A&E if someone with measles has a seizure, has severe difficulty breathing, cannot stay awake, is limp or floppy, has a stiff neck, or has a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it.

Measles is unlikely in anyone who has had both doses of the MMR or MMRV vaccine, or who has had measles before. Parents unsure whether their child is fully vaccinated can ask their GP surgery, which can give missed doses free on the NHS.

articles.title: Rochdale's pathology teams support millions of tests during National Pathology Week
articles.excerpt: As National Pathology Week is celebrated, Rochdale's pathology teams highlight their vital role in healthcare, processing over 10 million samples annually.
articles.content_html:
This week marks National Pathology Week, a time to recognise the essential work of pathology teams across Greater Manchester, including those in Rochdale.

These teams process more than 10 million samples and conduct over 35 million tests each year, playing a crucial role in patient care.

Pathology services are integral to approximately 95% of clinical pathways, providing the diagnostic information that clinicians rely on to diagnose illnesses, guide treatments, and monitor ongoing care. Despite their critical role, many patients may never meet the professionals working behind the scenes in pathology laboratories.

The Northern Care Alliance's pathology workforce includes nearly 700 staff members across various locations, including Rochdale, Oldham, Salford, and Bury. This diverse team comprises biomedical scientists, pathologists, clinical scientists, and other specialists who work together to ensure efficient and accurate testing.

Recent advancements in technology, such as the introduction of automated biopsy processing in Oldham, have improved workflow and increased capacity, allowing biomedical scientists to focus more on specialised diagnostic work.

As the healthcare landscape evolves, the importance of pathology services in supporting patient care continues to grow. The implementation of a new Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) has also transformed how laboratories manage samples and results, ensuring uninterrupted services for patients.

articles.excerpt: Steven's remarkable journey to lose 15 stone has transformed his health and confidence, allowing him to enjoy life with his family.
articles.content_html:
Steven, a member of Heywood Sports Village, has achieved a remarkable transformation by losing 15 stone, significantly improving his health and quality of life. His journey began when he realised that everyday activities had become increasingly difficult, impacting his ability to enjoy family life.

At his heaviest, Steven struggled with simple tasks such as walking upstairs and playing with his children. The turning point came after witnessing his wife's successful health transformation, which inspired him to take control of his own wellbeing.

He sought guidance from Personal Trainer Alex at Heywood Sports Village, where he received structured training and nutritional support.

Throughout his journey, Steven faced challenges, including moments when motivation dipped. However, the support from his family and the gym community helped him stay focused on his long-term goals.

Today, he feels fitter, stronger, and more confident, enjoying activities that were once daunting. He can now buy clothes from regular high street shops and participate in family holidays without feeling self-conscious.

Steven advises others looking to start their fitness journey to make small changes and set clear personal goals. He emphasises the importance of seeking support and working with a coach to achieve lasting results.

articles.title: Rochdale mum diagnosed with breast cancer after routine NHS screening
articles.excerpt: Sarah Hickman, 50, encourages women to attend NHS breast screenings after her cancer was detected early during a routine mammogram.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale mother, Sarah Hickman, has been diagnosed with breast cancer following a routine NHS screening, prompting her to urge other women to attend their appointments. At 50 years old, Sarah received her invitation for a mammogram and attended without any health concerns. However, just a day later, she was called back for further tests at the Breast Unit at Bolton NHS Foundation Trust.

After undergoing additional imaging, an ultrasound, and a biopsy, doctors confirmed that Sarah had a small breast cancer detected at a very early stage.

Reflecting on her experience, she described it as a 'textbook case' and expressed gratitude for the NHS screening process, which allowed for early detection before any symptoms appeared.

Sarah's case highlights the importance of regular breast screenings, especially for women aged 50 and over, who are invited for routine mammograms every three years. Early detection can significantly improve treatment outcomes and survival rates, making it crucial for women to take these invitations seriously.

As Sarah continues her treatment, she hopes her story will encourage others to prioritise their health and attend NHS screenings.

articles.title: Rochdale selected for £9.4m children’s mental health pilot
articles.excerpt: Breaking: Rochdale will join Stockport and Tameside in Care Together, bringing NHS mental health professionals into children’s social care teams from early 2027.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale has been selected for a new government mental health pilot designed to make support easier to access for children involved with social care and their families.

The Department of Health and Social Care has announced up to £9.4 million over three years for Care Together, which will operate across Rochdale, Stockport and Tameside.

Mental health professionals from existing NHS services will work within children's social care teams. The aim is to help families receive expert support earlier, with less difficulty navigating separate services.

NHS Greater Manchester Integrated Care Board will lead the programme alongside the three local authorities. It is expected to launch in early 2027 and run until 2029.

Who could benefit?

The department says up to 7,000 children and young people across the three participating boroughs could be covered, alongside their parents, carers and guardians. That figure covers all three boroughs combined. A separate allocation for Rochdale has not been provided in the announcement.

The groups identified include children in need, those on child protection plans, children in care, care leavers and adopted children.

Support could include family therapy and help for parents and primary caregivers, with services tailored to individual needs.

What will change for families?

Mental health professionals will work within social care settings, bringing expertise into the teams already supporting children and families.

The government hopes this will make it easier to identify needs and arrange appropriate help before problems reach crisis point. Faster access is an intended benefit of the pilot, with its effectiveness to be evaluated during the programme.

Dame Diana Johnson, Minister of State for Public Health and Patient Safety, said:

“For too long, fragmented mental health services have left young people in care, care leavers, parents, carers, and guardians not knowing where to turn for support.

“We are committed to change how we support young people, and this exciting and innovative pilot will see thousands more children across Greater Manchester get specialist mental health support based on their personal needs and in quicker time, before they reach crisis point.”

Children's Minister Josh MacAlister said children supported by social care can face severe mental health challenges because of trauma and adversity. He said the pilot forms part of wider efforts to support vulnerable young people as they move into adult life.

Professor Manisha Kumar, Chief Clinical Officer at NHS Greater Manchester, said the programme would help partners provide earlier support that takes account of children's experiences and wider family circumstances.

She said learning from the work in Rochdale, Stockport and Tameside would also help shape changes nationally.

When will Care Together start?

The pilot is expected to launch in early 2027 and run until 2029. An evaluation will assess whether the approach could be extended to other parts of the country.

The announcement does not yet specify how many Rochdale families will receive support, how referrals will work or which local teams will take part.

For local families, those practical details will matter: who can access help, how quickly it becomes available and whether bringing services together makes support easier to obtain.

articles.title: East Lancashire Railway secures portable defibrillator for its trains
articles.excerpt: The heritage railway serving Heywood plans to take lifesaving equipment onboard and is seeking support for more mobile units.
articles.content_html:
East Lancashire Railway has secured a portable defibrillator that will eventually travel on its trains, bringing potentially lifesaving equipment closer to passengers, staff and volunteers.

The heritage railway, which serves Heywood, received the Automated External Defibrillator (AED) following fundraising led by ELR Fund Raising Lead Adrian Dewey with support from national charity AEDdonate.

The unit is intended to move with train services rather than remain at a fixed location. It has not yet entered operational service. The railway says it will first establish arrangements for governance, asset management, equipment checks, training and deployment so it can be managed safely as it moves between services.

The new equipment will complement defibrillators already located at stations. ELR hopes to secure further mobile units, with the longer term ambition of extending coverage across all its operating services.

Chairman Mike Kelly said: “Keeping staff, volunteers and our visitors safe is our top priority. I want to thank AEDdonate for their timely donation and all of our kind donors for making this possible.”

He said having equipment available on trains, in addition to station defibrillators, would further strengthen the railway’s health and safety arrangements.

Phillip Warren, ELR Commercial Services Director and AED sponsor, said: “This is about putting lifesaving equipment where our passengers, volunteers and staff actually are.”

He explained that passengers may be travelling somewhere along the line rather than sitting beside a station building, making a portable unit an important additional resource in an onboard emergency.

“Hopefully this equipment will never be needed, but if that day ever comes, we want to have done everything reasonably possible to be prepared,” he said.

The announcement comes during Restart a Heart activity this October. The annual initiative, led by Resuscitation Council UK, promotes awareness of cardiac arrest and CPR education, with Restart a Heart Day held on 16 October.

As a registered charity, ELR relies on fundraising, donations, volunteers and support from businesses and other organisations. It is now inviting individuals to contribute to the next phase of the mobile AED project and businesses to consider sponsoring equipment.

Medical suppliers and other organisations able to donate a unit are also being encouraged to contact the railway.

Warren said: “It is a very tangible way of supporting a charity and potentially helping to save a life.”

Donations towards additional mobile defibrillators can be made through the ELR fundraising campaign: https://www.justgiving.com/campaign/elr-defibrilator-fundraiser

articles.title: Springhill Hospice to host free will information clinic in Heywood
articles.excerpt: Springhill Hospice is offering a free information clinic for those looking to make or update their wills, with expert guidance available.
articles.content_html:
Springhill Hospice will hold a free information clinic aimed at individuals considering making or updating their wills.

The event will take place at the hospice, providing an opportunity for attendees to learn about the importance of having a will and to ask questions regarding the process.

David Copeland, a solicitor from Molesworths Solicitors based in Rochdale, will lead the session. Participants will receive a free will template and refreshments will be provided.

The clinic is designed for anyone, whether they are making their first will or looking to amend an existing one.

Charlotte Mascarenhas, supporter engagement fundraiser at Springhill Hospice, emphasised that the clinic aims to simplify the process of formalising a will, which can often feel daunting for many.

Molesworths Solicitors will waive their usual fees for this service, requesting only a donation to the hospice in return. Springhill Hospice offers care for adults with life-limiting conditions and support for their families across Heywood, Middleton, and Rochdale.

The clinic is open to the public, and there is no obligation to engage further services. Those interested in attending are encouraged to reach out to Springhill Hospice for more details.

articles.title: From teaching assistant to PT: how Rochdale mum Jen Daker found the strongest version of herself
articles.excerpt: After 16 years in education, mum-of-two Jen Daker has found a new calling as a personal trainer at The Hybrid Hut in Rochdale, combining 4am discipline, family life and a passion for helping others build confidence.
articles.content_html:
There is an obvious physical transformation in Jen Daker’s story.

She is in the best shape of her life, trains with formidable discipline and has built a new career around fitness.

But Jen’s transformation goes far beyond how she looks.

For 16 years, Jen worked at the same school as a teaching assistant. She loved education, loved working with children and, for most of her adult working life, it was all she had known.

Then she became a mum.

After two pregnancies, her priorities began to change. Fitness, which had always been part of her life, became increasingly important not simply for how she looked, but for how she felt.

“I loved working in education, but after having children my priorities changed,” she said. “Fitness helped me so much physically and mentally after two pregnancies. I realised that if I could help other people feel like that, that was what I wanted to do.”

At 36, with two young children and a mortgage, changing careers was not the easy option.

Jen did it anyway.

Today she is a personal trainer at The Hybrid Hut in Rochdale, working with women and men of different ages, abilities and levels of confidence.

At the heart of her approach is one simple principle: consistency matters more than perfection.

Jen gets up at 4am to train.

There are mornings when staying in bed would be considerably easier, particularly after a broken night with the children.

But before school runs, clients, work and everything else involved in raising a family begins, Jen deliberately creates time that belongs to her.

“My workout isn’t just about keeping fit — it’s my time,” she said. “Before the school runs, work and everything else that comes with being a mum, I get an hour that’s just for me.”

Training first thing sets the tone for the rest of her day. She feels more energetic, her mood improves and she has already done something positive for herself before everybody else begins needing her.

It is an impressive level of discipline, but Jen is quick to point out that she does not wake every morning overflowing with motivation.

“Motivation comes and goes, but habits keep you going,” she said. “Some workouts are amazing and some aren’t. Showing up is what matters.”

That is also what she wants her clients to understand.

A healthy life is not built from one heroic gym session or one perfect week.

It is built from the ordinary things repeated often enough to matter. One walk. One healthier meal. One short workout. Then another.

Jen is equally clear that she did not make such a dramatic change alone.

Behind the early mornings, late evenings and weekend sessions is a family finding ways to make it work — and she credits her partner Damien as one of the central reasons she has been able to pursue it.

“I honestly couldn’t have made such a huge career change at 36, with two young children and a mortgage, without Damien,” she said.

“There are early mornings, late evenings and weekends where we’re juggling family life around work. Having someone who believes in you, encourages you and helps share the load makes such a difference.”

Her family, she says, have supported her from day one.

That strong relationship with Damien and her obvious love for her children sit at the centre of the life she has built rather than competing with it.

Jen does not pretend the balance is effortless. Some weeks work better than others.

“I’m still figuring it out,” she said. “I’ve learnt that looking after myself isn’t selfish — it’s necessary.”

Sometimes that means a workout. Sometimes a walk. Sometimes simply finding enough time for a quiet coffee.

For Jen, exercise has increasingly become about mental wellbeing.

She describes herself as having an active mind and says she can struggle to switch off. Exercise creates headspace.

“Life can feel hectic with work and children, and training gives me time to reset,” she said.

“It’s helped build my confidence and resilience. I don’t exercise because I want to look a certain way anymore. I do it because I know how much better I feel mentally when I move my body.”

But even someone capable of getting out of bed at 4am has had to learn that discipline is not the same thing as endlessly pushing harder.

There have been days when Jen has been exhausted or overwhelmed and recognised that another intense workout was not what her body needed.

Sometimes the healthier choice is a walk. Sometimes stretching. Sometimes rest.

“Listening to your body is just as important as pushing yourself,” she said. “Fitness should support your wellbeing, not become another source of pressure.”

She admits she is still learning to follow that advice herself.

Jen’s attitude towards food is similarly grounded in real life.

She loves food. Nothing is completely off limits.

And she does not want clients spending their lives bouncing between restrictive diets and guilt.

Her philosophy is that a healthy lifestyle must still leave room for birthdays, holidays, meals out and the foods people genuinely enjoy.

“One meal or one night out doesn’t undo months of healthy habits, just like one salad doesn’t suddenly make someone healthy,” she said.

“Food shouldn’t come with guilt.”

Instead, Jen encourages moderation and habits people can realistically sustain.

“Consistency wins every time. It’s what you do most of the time that matters, not what you do occasionally.

“Celebrate birthdays, enjoy holidays and make memories. Then just get back to your normal routine afterwards.”

There is no waiting for Monday. No declaring the month ruined because of one bad day.

“It’s never too late to start again,” Jen said. “Make your next choice a positive one and keep moving forward.”

Some of Jen’s proudest results cannot be measured with scales or photographed in a mirror.

One of her earliest clients found her after seeing a recommendation on Facebook. The pair had never met.

The woman had never even been inside a gym and arrived nervous and lacking confidence.

Over time, that changed. She began trusting herself. She became comfortable training. Eventually, while Jen was away on holiday, she went to the gym on her own — something she once would never have imagined doing.

“She is like a totally different person to the woman I met,” Jen said.

For Jen, that is the real reward.

“I’ve met people who were scared to walk into a gym become confident enough to train on their own,” she said.

“Most of the time the biggest transformation isn’t physical — it’s the confidence they gain in every part of their lives.”

She sees that particularly among mothers.

Motherhood can be all-consuming. Somewhere among school runs, work, washing, appointments and everybody else’s needs, women can begin feeling that the person they once were has disappeared.

Jen understands that. And she loves watching them find themselves again.

There is another misconception Jen would happily dismantle: that personal trainers are endlessly confident.

She believes the reality can be almost the opposite.

Working every day in an environment where bodies and physical performance are constantly visible can make trainers highly critical of themselves if they allow it.

And they certainly are not expecting new clients to arrive already fit.

“Most trainers just want to help people improve, whatever their starting point is,” she said.

Jen even experienced nerves herself after recently returning from a two-week holiday.

“I got the pre-gym nerves going back,” she said.

Her message to somebody frightened of walking into a gym for the first time is straightforward. Almost everybody has felt like that. Most other people are concentrating on their own workout, not watching yours.

“Every confident person in the gym was a beginner once,” Jen said. “The hardest part is walking through the door.”

There is perhaps no such thing as perfectly balancing motherhood, relationships, work, health, friendships and everything else expected of women.

Some days one thing will inevitably win.

But Jen Daker’s story suggests women can get remarkably close.

Today, Jen offers one-to-one personal training, small-group sessions and tailored online fitness plans, working with people of all ages and abilities.

She describes The Hybrid Hut as a gym where beginners, experienced athletes, younger people and older clients are all equally welcome.

Train with Jen Daker at The Hybrid Hut.

The Hybrid Hut, Unit 1A, Moss Mill Street / Woodbine Street East Industrial Estate, Rochdale, OL16 5LB. Telephone: 07547 619709. Jen can also be contacted through her Instagram and Facebook pages, or by visiting The Hybrid Hut in Rochdale.

articles.title: One urgent care centre for 220,000 people: does Rochdale not deserve a real hospital?
articles.excerpt: Fifteen years after losing its A&E and maternity unit, Rochdale relies on a minor-injuries urgent care centre while its emergencies travel to Bury, Oldham and Manchester. Research shows distance to emergency care carries a measurable mortality risk.
articles.content_html:
A borough of 220,000 people. One urgent care facility. No A&E, no maternity unit, no children's ward. Is that really adequate for Rochdale?

Rochdale Infirmary is open, and its staff do valuable work. The Whitehall Street site runs a 24/7 Urgent Care Centre, a short-stay Clinical Assessment Unit, day surgery, a rheumatology centre, x-ray, blood testing, antenatal clinics, an early pregnancy unit, outpatient clinics and an eye unit. But the NHS's own description is blunt: there is no A&E at Rochdale Infirmary. The Urgent Care Centre treats minor injury and illness. It is the fourth smallest hospital in the Northern Care Alliance.

That is what remains of a hospital that, within living memory, was a proper district general. The A&E department closed in 2011. The maternity unit went the same way, along with the children's ward and, over the past two decades, ward after ward of acute provision - each removal justified at the time as centralisation, each leaving Rochdale residents travelling further for care.

Today, a Rochdale resident with a genuine emergency is sent to Fairfield in Bury, the Royal Oldham, or North Manchester General. On a good day, that is a manageable journey. In an ambulance queue, at rush hour, or for a family without a car relying on two buses, it is anything but. Every expectant mother in the borough gives birth outside it.

Does distance cost lives? The honest answer is that nobody publishes a Rochdale-specific figure, and we will not invent one. No official body calculates the percentage of local deaths that could have been avoided if a full hospital were closer, and any number we quoted would be guesswork. What does exist is peer-reviewed national research. A study of over 10,000 life-threatening emergency cases, published in the Emergency Medicine Journal by University of Sheffield researchers, found that the risk of death rose as the journey to hospital lengthened - from 5.8% for patients living under 10km away to 8.8% for those more than 20km away, with each additional 10km associated with around a one percentage point increase in mortality. Distance to emergency care is not a neutral fact. It is a clinical risk factor.

That research does not prove any individual Rochdale death was avoidable. It does mean the burden of proof should sit with those who decided that a borough of 220,000 people - larger than many towns and cities with a full district general hospital - can safely be served by a minor injuries facility.

The underuse of the Infirmary compounds the frustration. The site exists. The buildings exist. A workforce exists. Yet its role has been steadily narrowed rather than rebuilt, even as the borough's population has grown and the hospitals absorbing Rochdale's emergencies report some of the longest waits in the country. If capacity across north-east Greater Manchester is the problem - and A&E waiting figures suggest it is - then an under-used hospital estate in the middle of a 220,000-person borough looks less like a rational configuration and more like an inherited decision nobody has had the courage to revisit.

We asked whether the borough's elected representatives have taken a public position on restoring acute services to the Infirmary. We could find no current on-record statements from the borough's MPs or councillors specifically committing to that goal, and rather than paraphrase old campaign material we have chosen to put the question directly: does Rochdale's political leadership believe the current provision is adequate for this borough - and if not, what are they doing about it? We will publish their answers in full.

Fifteen years on from losing its A&E, the question for Rochdale is no longer how the services went, but why a borough this size should not expect them back. A fully equipped hospital - with an emergency department, a maternity unit and the wards this town has lost - is not nostalgia. For 220,000 people, it is the level of provision most comparable boroughs would consider a baseline.

If you are seriously ill or injured, always call 999 or attend your nearest A&E. The Urgent Care Centre at Rochdale Infirmary remains open 24/7 for minor injuries and illness, and NHS 111 can advise on the right service.

articles.title: Rainbow Health Group invites residents to open day at new clinic after 17 years on Hornby Street
articles.excerpt: The health and wellbeing clinic is moving to a new home after 17 years, and is welcoming the community to an open day this Saturday - with the Mayor and Mayoress performing the official opening at 1pm.
articles.content_html:
A local health and wellbeing clinic is inviting Milnrow and Newhey residents - and anyone else who fancies a look around - to celebrate the start of a new chapter this weekend.

After 17 years at its Hornby Street clinic, Rainbow Health Group is moving to a brand-new home, and is holding an open day on Saturday 8 August from 11am to 3pm to welcome the community through the doors.

The clinic offers a range of treatments including sports massage, clinical massage, acupuncture, K-Laser therapy, podiatry and rehabilitation, helping people recover from injuries, manage pain and improve their overall wellbeing.

Its new address is Unit 9A, Southgate Industrial Park, Green Lane, Heywood, OL10 1ND.

Visitors on the day can explore the new clinic, meet the team, and learn more about the treatments and services on offer, with complimentary light refreshments provided. There will also be a charity raffle in aid of Help 4 All, and the Mayor and Mayoress will officially open the clinic at 1pm.

"Whether you've been visiting us for years or have never heard of Rainbow Health Group before, everyone is welcome," the clinic said. "We'd love to see you there and celebrate this exciting new chapter with our local community."

articles.title: Every GP practice in Rochdale ranked by patients in the 2026 survey
articles.excerpt: The latest GP Patient Survey shows a wide gap in reported patient experience between practices across Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough and Milnrow.
articles.content_html:
Patients have rated their experiences at GP practices across Rochdale borough in the latest national survey, revealing a wide difference between the highest and lowest results recorded on one key measure.

Rochdale Daily compared practices using the percentage of respondents who described their overall experience of their GP practice as good in the 2026 GP Patient Survey.

Dr GWD Bhima recorded the highest result among the borough practices included in the comparison, with 96.2 per cent of respondents reporting a good overall experience. Milnrow Village Practice followed on 95.4 per cent, with The Village Medical Centre in Littleborough on 94 per cent.

At the other end of the comparison, Croft Shifa Health Centre recorded 44.9 per cent. The difference between the highest and lowest results was therefore 51.3 percentage points.

The England figure was 76.7 per cent.

WHAT THE FIGURES SHOW

The results show substantial variation both across the borough and within individual townships. Heywood practices ranged from 91.8 per cent at Birtle View Medical Practice to 66.7 per cent at Heywood Health.

WHAT THE COMPARISON DOES NOT MEAN

The GP Patient Survey is based on a sample of registered patients, rather than every patient at each practice. Results are weighted, but smaller samples carry greater statistical uncertainty and practices serve populations with different needs and circumstances.

NHS England and Ipsos advise that the survey was not designed to create a definitive league table of GP practices. The ordering above is therefore a straightforward comparison of the published overall-experience percentage, not a declaration that one practice provides objectively better clinical care than another.

The 2026 survey was conducted between 2 January and 13 April and published on 9 July. Practices may have introduced changes since patients completed their questionnaires.

articles.title: Is this how the NHS treats its own? 81-year-old man left outside Rochdale Infirmary for ten hours
articles.excerpt: An 81-year-old man spent around ten hours lying outside Rochdale Infirmary while members of the public repeatedly sought help. Rochdale Daily investigates what happened and asks who held responsibility for his care.
articles.content_html:
An 81-year-old man lay confused, incoherent and unable to stand outside the grounds of Rochdale Infirmary for around ten hours while members of the public desperately tried to persuade the emergency services, hospital staff and social care agencies to help him.

The disturbing incident was witnessed and filmed by the editor of Rochdale Daily, who saw passers-by provide the man with water, blankets, cushions, food and cardboard while repeated attempts were made to establish which public service had responsibility for his welfare.

The man was found lying on the ground near the hospital car park. He appeared unable to stand unaided and could rarely string together more than two words. He later told those attempting to assist him that he was 81 years old.

Security staff were monitoring the situation and informed members of the public they had contacted Greater Manchester Police. Officers did not arrive until approximately ten hours after the ordeal began.

Members of the public repeatedly attempted to request an ambulance. During those calls, callers say they were informed the man was barred from the ambulance service because of previous behaviour and because of other matters that could not be discussed due to data protection legislation.

The precise legal status of any restriction involving the man has not yet been independently confirmed. However, Rochdale Daily holds video footage of the day's events, including numerous conversations between witnesses, members of the public and staff.

Whatever may have happened previously, the man lying on the ground that day appeared incapable of posing any immediate threat. He was confused, unable to stand, largely unable to communicate and repeatedly soiled himself while lying outside the hospital.

Members of the public also attempted to contact Rochdale Council Adult Social Care, people believed to be relatives, homelessness organisations and local charities. Appeals were placed on Facebook asking whether anyone knew the gentleman or could help locate family members.

Some comments on social media suggested the man had brought the situation upon himself if he had previously abused NHS staff. One commenter wrote: "You don't get barred from the NHS for nothing."

No one should minimise the abuse suffered by NHS workers. Nurses, doctors, paramedics, receptionists and security staff face unacceptable levels of violence, intimidation and verbal abuse every day. Staff deserve protection, and where individuals genuinely pose a danger, organisations are entitled to implement appropriate safeguards.

But that was not the man witnessed by Rochdale Daily.

For hour after hour he remained lying on the ground, unable to stand, struggling to communicate and apparently incapable of caring for himself. Members of the public did not witness any aggression towards staff, security or those trying to help him.

Throughout the day, ambulance vehicles entered and left the hospital site. Witnesses attempted to flag them down, but the vehicles continued past. Others reportedly stopped only to explain they were unable to assist.

Approximately six hours into the incident, two nurses accompanied by hospital security entered the car park and spoke with those attempting to help the man.

According to the editor's contemporaneous video recording, the nurses stated they could not treat the gentleman unless the situation became a matter of "life or death".

When asked what 'life or death' would look like to an untrained member of the public, they replied: "We couldn't tell you."

Members of the public then asked whose duty of care the gentleman fell under if he died while no organisation would intervene. One member of staff replied: "Not you."

When pressed as to which organisation would carry responsibility if treatment continued to be refused, those present say no clear answer was given.

One nurse then stated that the gentleman's breathing would have to stop before intervention could take place.

The editor replied that she could not see him breathing. The nurse looked over the wall towards the gentleman and responded that his chest was rising and therefore he was breathing.

During the exchange, one nurse was recorded saying: "This is what you get when you're on it day and night."

When asked what she meant by the remark, no explanation was given.

Later in the incident, a person identifying themselves as a family member stated the gentleman had dementia. Rochdale Daily has not independently verified that relationship or medical diagnosis.

A representative from Get Together After Serving CIC attended the scene after becoming aware of the incident and also attempted to secure medical assistance.

The representative said they were informed the gentleman was subject to a restraining order involving the Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust and that members of the public would need to transport him outside the area before treatment could be sought elsewhere.

Rochdale Daily has requested clarification from the Trust regarding that alleged restriction.

Throughout the ordeal, members of the public continued caring for the gentleman. Bottles of water, blankets, cushions, cardboard and food were brought to make him more comfortable while people searched desperately for someone willing to take responsibility.

Among the organisations contacted, only Get Together After Serving CIC and Hebron Pentecostal Church attended to assist.

Approximately ten hours after the incident began, police officers attended the scene.

The following morning, disposable cups, bowls and cardboard still marked the place where the elderly man had spent much of the previous day.

This investigation is not an argument that NHS staff should tolerate abuse. They should not. Nor is it an argument that previous violent or abusive behaviour should simply be ignored.

It is, however, a question of safeguarding.

If an elderly man is confused, apparently incapable of caring for himself, unable to stand, repeatedly soiling himself and lying outside the grounds of a hospital, who has responsibility for protecting him?

If previous behaviour has resulted in restrictions, what emergency pathway exists when that same individual later appears to lack capacity or requires urgent medical assessment?

Those are questions Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust, North West Ambulance Service, Greater Manchester Police and Rochdale Council's Adult Social Care service should now answer.

Rochdale Daily has contacted all relevant organisations for comment and will publish their responses in full when received.

Until then, one unavoidable question remains.

Is this how the NHS treats its own?

articles.title: Is ketamine becoming a problem in Rochdale? Health leaders warn of a growing concern
articles.excerpt: Health professionals are warning of the growing harms associated with ketamine as national use rises. But what does the picture look like in Rochdale, and why are experts becoming increasingly concerned?
articles.content_html:
Ketamine was once regarded primarily as a nightclub drug, but health professionals, police and addiction specialists say its use has changed dramatically over the past decade. Increasingly, the drug is being used by younger people in a wider range of settings, prompting growing concern about its impact on physical and mental health.

While there is no publicly available evidence to suggest Rochdale has a ketamine problem significantly worse than other parts of Greater Manchester, local authorities recognise substance misuse as an important public health issue and have included drug-related harm as a key priority in the borough's long-term prevention strategy. Rochdale's Preventing Drug and Alcohol Harm Strategy highlights the need to reduce drug-related harm through prevention, early intervention, treatment and recovery services.

Ketamine is a Class B controlled drug in the UK. Originally developed as a medical anaesthetic, it produces feelings of detachment and hallucinations when used recreationally. In recent years, it has become increasingly popular because it is often cheaper than cocaine and MDMA, while users mistakenly believe it to be a 'safer' drug.

National evidence suggests that perception is dangerously wrong. The Home Office's latest wastewater analysis estimates ketamine consumption has increased substantially in England in recent years, making it one of the country's most commonly consumed illegal drugs after cocaine.

Doctors are particularly concerned about the long-term physical effects. Repeated ketamine use can cause irreversible damage to the bladder and urinary tract, a condition sometimes referred to as 'ketamine bladder' or ketamine-induced cystitis. Heavy users may experience severe pain, frequent urination, bleeding and, in the most serious cases, permanent bladder damage requiring reconstructive surgery. Medical specialists have reported a significant increase in young patients requiring treatment for these complications.

Mental health professionals also warn that regular ketamine use can lead to dependency, memory problems, anxiety, depression and episodes of psychosis in some individuals. Because the drug affects perception and coordination, users are also at increased risk of accidents, injuries and dangerous behaviour while intoxicated.

Locally, Rochdale Borough Council's Joint Strategic Needs Assessment identifies substance misuse among young adults as an ongoing public health challenge. Hospital admission rates linked to substance misuse among young people remain broadly similar to the national average, while the council notes that vulnerable groups are at greater risk of developing drug-related problems.

Although official figures are not routinely broken down by individual drug at borough level, professionals working in addiction services across Greater Manchester say ketamine now features far more frequently than it did a decade ago. Nationally, the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs concluded earlier this year that misuse is increasing and recommended strengthening education, prevention and treatment services while keeping ketamine as a Class B drug.

Parents are encouraged to be aware of the warning signs. These can include sudden mood changes, poor concentration, unexplained urinary problems, nosebleeds caused by snorting powder, secrecy around friendships, declining school or college attendance and unexplained financial difficulties. None of these signs alone necessarily indicate drug use, but experts advise early conversations and support where concerns exist.

Support is available for anyone struggling with drug use. Rochdale residents can access confidential help through local drug and alcohol treatment services without fear of judgement. Health professionals stress that seeking support early greatly improves the chances of recovery and helps prevent long-term physical damage.

The message from health leaders is clear. While ketamine may still carry an image as a recreational party drug, the evidence increasingly shows it can have devastating consequences for both physical and mental health. Prevention, education and early intervention remain the most effective ways of protecting young people across Rochdale borough from the lasting harm associated with its misuse.
